seasons.review_body: Bodkin premiered May 9, 2024 as a Netflix Irish black comedy created by Jez Scharf. Will Forte plays Gilbert Power, an American podcaster who travels to the Irish coastal village of Bodkin to investigate the 30-year-old disappearance of three people during a Samhain festival. He is joined by an Irish investigative journalist (Siobhan Cullen) and a researcher (Robyn Cara). Critics approved at 68 percent from 40 reviews, crediting the show's satirical edge on true-crime media consumption and the distinct eccentricity of its Irish setting and characters. The consensus reservation - that the underlying mystery is too thin to sustain seven episodes - was repeated across multiple reviews. The show is more interested in its satirical mode than its genre mechanics, which is either a strength or a limitation.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# Bodkin S1E1: "Part One: American in Ireland" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The first body arrives by phone. **Dove** is told her key informant has hanged himself, and the news does not stop her. It sharpens her. Within minutes, the episode has her reject Ireland, reject the assignment, and reject the podcast format before moving toward the story she claims to want no part of. That is the hour’s best trick: everyone announces a clean position, then Bodkin dirties it. The mystery is old. The habits are not.

## Dove Runs From the Case by Walking Into It

“Part One: American in Ireland” works best when it treats refusal as action. Dove begins the hour in damage mode. Her informant is dead, the warning around her is clear, and her answer is to keep working. She pushes against Ireland before the trip even takes shape, asking why they would return there, but the scene has already trapped her. The more she resists, the more the story pulls her in.

That contradiction gives the premiere its spine. Dove says no with the posture of someone who has already started saying yes. The assignment to a true crime podcast is framed as an insult to her seriousness, yet the episode does not let that contempt stay pure. Once the Samhain mystery is named, her investigative reflexes begin eating through her objections.

The writing is sharpest in that early turn because it keeps Dove abrasive, suspicious, and professionally restless. Her grief over the informant does not become a speech. It becomes velocity. The hour understands that a reporter who refuses to stop can look brave from one angle and reckless from another. Dove is working before she admits she is working.

## The Podcast Wants a Story, the Town Smells a Raid

**Gilbert Power** enters with the easy self-branding of a man who knows how to introduce himself. He is the podcaster, the person who can turn absence into episodes and old grief into structure. His pull is the mystery itself: what happened, why the festival got blamed, and what meaning can be recovered from a village’s buried panic.

That makes him a useful counterweight to Dove. He is chasing shape. Bodkin’s premiere uses him to make podcasting a method with built-in danger. A story needs rapport. An investigation needs pressure. The hour keeps rubbing those impulses together until sparks show.

The Samhain case gives the setup a clean hook. At Ailbhe’s Hollow, the group lays out the disappearances from 25 years ago. Three people vanished, and the old explanation still hangs in the air like bad weather. Later, in the bar, a stranger angle enters the bloodstream: the missing were attacked by horses. It is the kind of detail a true crime story loves because it sounds absurd until a town repeats it with a straight face.

Some of this setup arrives in tidy blocks. There are stretches where people explain the case more than they fight over it. Still, the central design holds. Gilbert wants meaning. Dove wants truth under duress. Bodkin knows those are different jobs.

## Emmy Learns the Wrong Lesson Fast

The premiere’s most interesting contradiction belongs to **Emmy Sizergh**. She begins as the digital-department professional who treats the work as contact, access, and storytelling. Her mode is rapport. She understands that a podcast is built out of people talking, and she sees herself as the person who can keep the human machinery running when Dove’s bluntness threatens to break it.

Then she finds the folder.

That late discovery inside **Sergeant Ruairi Power**’s house gives the episode its cleanest character snap. Emmy’s position collapses the moment there is something physical to take. A folder from the year of the Samhain disappearances is evidence-shaped. Emmy steals it, and the act makes a joke of her own professional boundary.

This is where the hour earns its best tension. Emmy does something Dove-like while still carrying Emmy’s need to be useful and included. The theft is clumsy because it should be clumsy. It is a person trying on investigative trespass before she has learned its cost.

The episode could have pushed harder into her panic after the discovery. The beat lands, but it arrives with more plot efficiency than emotional mess. Even so, the turn matters. The show’s softest character crosses the clearest line. Suddenly, the podcast is contaminating Bodkin.

## Sergeant Power Is the Wall, Not the Villain

Sergeant Ruairi Power’s function in the premiere is simple and effective: he is the town saying stop. He confronts the group about snooping and pushes them to drop the podcast. The writing does not need to make him theatrically sinister. His resistance carries enough charge because the case is already unstable.

A flatter version of this hour would make the local authority a locked door with a badge. Bodkin gives him practical force. He has history with the case, possession of the old folder, and a clear interest in preventing outsiders from turning Samhain into content. The premiere leaves the nature of that interest open. Protective, guilty, exhausted, tangled. Any of those can play.

That uncertainty matters because the episode is built around competing versions of intrusion. Dove intrudes through pressure. Gilbert intrudes through narrative hunger. Emmy intrudes by pretending she is there to smooth things over, then leaves with the folder. Sergeant Power’s warning becomes more than obstruction. It is a moral accusation.

The hour’s silences help here. The rhythm is uneven in places, with stretches that feel like resets before confrontations, but the pauses give the town resistance. Bodkin does not chatter through every gap. Sometimes it lets a room refuse to help. For a mystery about old disappearances, that refusal gives the atmosphere weight.

## The Horse Story Is Ridiculous Enough to Work

The bar conversation about horses attacking the disappeared is the premiere’s strangest gift. It sounds like local nonsense, but the episode treats it as a clue-shaped distortion rather than a punchline. That matters. The Samhain mystery needs folklore without turning into fog machine television, and this beat gives it practical weirdness.

The claim also reframes the case. If the disappeared were attacked, then the town’s old explanation involves violence, memory, and whatever story people invent when the real one is too ugly or too useful to say plainly. The horse detail may be false, but as local testimony, it tells the podcast team what kind of place they have entered. Bodkin is a town where explanations can be absurd and still socially functional.

This is where the premiere finds its flavor. The early scenes are procedural by design: a dead informant, an assignment, a reluctant trip, an old case. The horse beat cracks that surface. It brings in the warped comedy of rural rumor and the unease of a community that has had 25 years to rehearse its evasions.

The episode does not cash that oddness yet. It plants more than it pays. That is acceptable first-hour work, and this seed is ugly enough to remember.

## The Verdict

“Part One: American in Ireland” is a sturdy, prickly opener about people who think they can manage the story of the missing three. Dove gives the hour teeth. Gilbert’s podcast frame gives it shape. Emmy’s folder theft gives it the first real moral bruise. The weakness is pacing: some case setup lands too neatly, and the episode occasionally pauses when it should tighten. Still, the premiere builds a useful engine. Bodkin begins as a mystery about Samhain, then makes the better move by turning investigation itself into the first crime scene. BollyAI’s read: a solid start with one excellent character contradiction and enough local strangeness to justify the return trip.

verdict.one_liner: A sturdy opener where Emmy’s stolen folder cuts sharper than the case briefing, even when the pacing loosens.
